item.text: {"text":"User–item deduplication retaining one event per pair removes observable same-item recurrence: multiplicity, repeat intervals, and repeat next-item targets disappear. Removing only identical records or consecutive duplicates has different effects; SASRec alone does not establish which preprocessing occurred. Amazon review records also cannot establish actual purchase frequency, and the dataset maintainers flag duplicate-review/item issues ([Amazon documentation](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~jmcauley/datasets/amazon_v2/index.html)). Consequently, measure per-category duplicate-event fractions and prefix-to-next-item repeat rates from permitted training histories. If pairs are globally unique, exact-item repeat weighting has no direct behavioral signal; any benefit would need another explanation.\n\nSeparate exact-ID recurrence from recurrence of learned interests. [RepeatNet](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/4408) explicitly gates between selecting previously observed items and exploring new items; its repeat branch requires surviving repeats and eligible seen-item candidates. For distinct-item interests, [ComiRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.09347) learns multiple interest vectors from interaction sequences through dynamic routing or self-attention, without requiring pretrained representations. A practical diagnostic extension is to learn item similarities or clusters using training-only co-occurrence or randomly initialized collaborative embeddings, then measure returns to the same cluster across distinct IDs, especially after intervening interests. Compare exact-item repetition, distinct-item cluster recurrence, and recency-only baselines. Cluster recurrence is evidence of recurring collaborative patterns, not proof of semantic interests or repurchases; evaluate any weighting through the fixed macro validation HR@10."}
